#1114. Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's  unfair trade practices.

In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.

Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue.

Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means."

China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction."

Before the COVID pandemic, the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent.

Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.

Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking, precision engineering and chemicals industries.

German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.

Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures.

In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.

"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.

Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."

Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:

"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.

According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.

While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.

The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.

Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."

Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.

Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on how many hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report.

Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.

Reports say the agreement would cap such Chinese imports at 350,000 vehicles annually, with the limit increasing by 6% each year over four years.

Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.

MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion (€354 billion), versus $172 billion to the US.

This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.

"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.

#1111. In Indonesia, PhD students blow the whistle on bad supervision

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

PhD students at Indonesian universities say that the quality of supervision in the nation is often poor, and that many supervisors engage in inappropriate behaviour.Credit: epsgalery85/Shutterstock

When Rully Charitas Prahmana went to the United States as a visiting lecturer, the academic culture shock was extreme. “I was surprised to see an academic supervisor go cycling with his PhD students on the weekend,” says Prahmana, a mathematics lecturer at Ahmad Dahlan University in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, and a visiting researcher at the Western Michigan University in Kalamazoo.

Prahmana can’t imagine that kind of interaction at home, describing himself as being in the minority for occasionally holding informal discussions with students in a warung, small street-food stalls or restaurants that are common across Indonesia. Many of his colleagues never meet their students in casual settings, he says.

PhD candidate–supervisor relationships in the southeast Asian archipelago nation are often less centred around direct scientific supervision in a laboratory or throughout a research project than in much of the rest of the world’s PhD programmes. Many early-career researchers instead say that they only meet supervisors for brief formal discussions, to sign research proposals, or to sign off on their dissertations. Students at larger and more prestigious institutions sometimes have more direct supervision, but “mostly, what we have is power asymmetry”, says Prahmana.

“I met my supervisors routinely but instead of supervising me, they were gossiping about other lecturers,” says one of 11 PhD students interviewed for this article. Several individuals requested anonymity to protect their careers.

Some described being asked to take on tasks at personal expense. One interviewee, for example, said that she had to pay for access to sampling sites before doing her wet-lab research. “I need to take out 200,000 rupiah [around US$12] every week for a year per sampling site,” says the student. All told, she was spending around $1,700 a year on her sampling work. The average monthly salary in Indonesia is around $200.

“I am sure there are many professors who treat students unfairly,” says an anonymous student in Semarang, Indonesia.

“But we are forced to accept what our supervisors say because we just want to graduate soon,” says another.

Some young academics argue that the problem of bad supervisors stems from poor management of PhD programmes in Indonesia, which aims to increase its population of doctoral graduates from around 75,000 to 125,000 by 2045. Brian Yuliarto, the nation’s minister for higher education, science and technology, says that this ambition will drive economic growth. National statistical data are patchy, with broad censuses every ten years, but Indonesia has an estimated 64 million people between the ages of 16 and 30. Yuliarto describes this group — 22% of the country’s population — as “a demography bonus”, telling Nature that the nation needs “to transform them into highly qualified human resources”.

Today in Indonesia, there are 272 PhD holders per one million people, compared with around 14,000 per million in the United States, for example.

My relationship with my PhD supervisor has become toxic — what do I do?

My relationship with my PhD supervisor has become toxic — what do I do?

To boost this number, the Indonesia Endowment Fund for Education, an agency that manages the country’s $9.1-million fund, has set aside money for another 2,500 PhD scholarships this year, says Yuliarto. Nearly half of these will be for those who want to pursue PhD opportunities overseas; the rest will be reserved for people studying partially or fully in Indonesia.

But only some Indonesian universities are set up to provide enough supervision to double the number of people graduating with high-quality PhDs, argues Berry Juliandi, dean of mathematics and natural sciences at IPB University in Bogor. He says that the new funding isn’t supported by strategic policies and regulations around improving academic supervision for the nation’s universities, which will therefore not be able to deliver a high-quality PhD experience.

Indonesia has 4,303 higher-education institutions. The country’s National Accreditation Agency for Higher Education counts only 226 of those as ‘highly qualified’, a criterion that accounts for the quality of not only the physical infrastructure, but also scientific prestige and experience and the teaching skills of the lecturers at the institutions.

Even at these institutions, conflicts between supervisors and PhD students are rife, says Fikri Yanda, a PhD student at Walailak University in Thai Buri, Thailand, who manages the ‘pembela_mahasiswa_indonesia’ (‘Indonesia student advocates’) Instagram account, which discusses academia in Indonesia.

Rully Charitas Prahmana, who teaches mathematics at Ahmad Dahlan University, in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, says that there is often a power asymmetry between PhD supervisors and students in Indonesia.Credit: Rully Charitas Indra Prahmana

So far this year, Indonesia’s ministry of education has reported 874 cases of inappropriate behaviour, including ethical misconduct, violence, sexual harassment and abuse of power.

This kind of behaviour “hampers our freedom to think freely as academics”, says Andik Wijayanto, a biology PhD student at Gadjah Mada University in Yogyakarta, because scientists aren’t able to challenge the status quo. Many students are afraid to make mistakes, he says. (Wijayanto, who also lectures in biology at the State University of Malang in East Java, says that he doesn’t have any problems with his own supervisors.)

In 2017, Indonesia’s higher-education ministry found that of 5,366 professors in Indonesia, 3,800 had not published peer-reviewed papers in international journals that the government considered reputable. This led to stricter regulations that now require all professors and other university lecturers with master’s and doctoral degrees of all disciplines to publish in high-quality Scopus-indexed journals. But the policy backfired: some academics were snared by predatory journals — organizations that offer to publish papers for a fee, often using aggressive or misleading solicitation practices, while not providing legitimate peer review or adequate editorial assistance. Other researchers manipulated their citation indexes to achieve high performance scores in the government’s evaluation system.

In 2021, the ministry introduced a regulation on scientific integrity that sanctions scientists who engage in data fabrication, plagiarism and forged authorship. This was followed by another regulation signed by Yuliarto this February, which asks institutions to assess ‘scientific integrity’ when evaluating university lecturers’ performance, a determining factor for their career opportunities.

#1110. World Cup qualifier suspended after sinkhole opens up on pitch

Play was brought to a standstill during Austriaâs 2026 World Cup qualifier against Cyprus after a sinkhole suddenly appeared on the pitch late in the second half.

The bizarre incident occurred around the 75th minute, when Danish referee Jakob Kehlet halted the match after noticing the gaping hole near Austria keeper Alexander Schlagerâs box at the Raiffeisen Arena, in Linz.

The opening was wide enough to swallow an entire football, prompting ground staff to rush on with buckets of sand in a frantic attempt to patch it up.

After more than seven minutes of repairs, Kehlet finally gave the green light to resume, with Austria eventually sealing a 1-0 win thanks to Marcel Sabitzerâs second-half penalty â scored before the ground gave way.

A section of the pitch has literally collapsed in the game between Austria & Cyprus. The ground staff are running up and down with buckets of soil trying to sort the situation. Canât remember seeing anything like it! pic.twitter.com/OECrF5jiGk

The win means Austria are now second in Group H qualifying, having won all three of their games so far, behind also unbeaten Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Remarkably, this isnât the first time Austrian football has flirted with the earth caving in. Back in 2022, a Nations League clash against Denmark, which Austria lost 2-1, at the Ernst Happel Stadium was also interrupted by a huge sinkhole opening up on the pitch.

At least this time Austria still managed to dig out the three points â though maybe someone in should be calling a geologist before the next fixture.

Unfortunately for Chelsea, Wesley Fofana put his hand up twice. Firstly to concede the first-half penalty for handball that allowed Liverpool to equalise quickly after Chelsea themselves had scored from the spot.

And secondly to volunteer to take one of the penalties in the shoot-out. The defender had to score to keep Chelsea in it, but he woefully, nervously skied his effort high into a gleeful Kop and it was Liverpool who went through to the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.

LIVERPOOL ARE THROUGH TO THE QUARTER-FINALS OF THE CARABAO CUP! 🔴 Wesley Fofana blazes over to hand Liverpool their FIFTH consecutive victory ✅ https://t.co/M4n01R8DSk

There the reward for Andoni Iraola, the head coach, is a home tie against the club he left in the summer: Bournemouth. The draw has opened up for Liverpool, and they know it, with only Manchester City left of the other big guns. But despite again playing at Anfield, they would have preferred not to face such a dangerous and motivated opponent, who have just reeled off five wins and five clean sheets in a row under Iraola’s replacement, Marco Rose.

This was also a big win. A meaningful win. One that was celebrated as such with Dua Lipa’s One Kiss – an anthem on Jürgen Klopp’s run to Liverpool’s first Champions League final under him in 2018 – played over the loudspeakers at the end as the players joyfully milled around the pitch.

One kiss is all it takes 🎶 https://t.co/0jfujy4V94

“I am happy to feel it. We feel the support,” Iraola said when asked whether he sensed the momentum and togetherness building in his reshaped Liverpool side. It looks as though they are.

Fofana was Chelsea’s eighth taker, so they were running out of options, but it was a truly terrible effort. The 25-year-old turned and scratched his head – just as many Chelsea fans have done over his underwhelming, albeit injury-hit, contributions since his eyebrow-raising £75m move from Leicester City in 2022.

Both sides had the chance to win it earlier in the shoot-out. For Liverpool it was Kostas Tsimikas, who had taken the decisive kick to beat Chelsea in a shoot-out in the 2022 FA Cup final, but the Greek full-back also completely missed the target.

Tsimikas has the chance to put Liverpool through... And fires over the bar! 😱 https://t.co/eCKBT6njMB

This was the fifth penalty shoot-out between these two clubs, in all competitions, with Liverpool having now triumphed in all five. They won the toss for this one and elected to take the kicks in front of the Kop, which roared its satisfaction and did its best to unsettle the Chelsea takers.

Both stand-in goalkeepers – Giorgi Mamardashvili and Mike Penders – made one outstanding save each in the shoot-out. Chelsea substitute Valentín Barco was the other player to miss, hitting a post.

Among Chelsea’s scorers was Jordan Henderson and the former Liverpool captain received a strange homecoming in his first appearance at Anfield for three years. He was booed, in the first half at least, and especially when he tucked the ball under his arm before Chelsea took their penalty – in normal time – which gave them the lead. Henderson turned to the stands, grinning.

Afterwards, Alonso faced more questions about his decision not to use Estêvão Willian. It was hardly a ringing endorsement especially as Alonso brought on Emegha instead. Virgil van Dijk was NOT HAPPY with Emmanuel Emegha 😒 https://t.co/UEtoJ7n5va

There is no VAR at this stage of the competition but referee Darren England appeared to get all the big calls right. Rogers claimed a penalty before Chelsea’s one was awarded, but Ronald Araújo was probably just too strong.

A word on VAR (again). Watching this competition without the presence of the joy-killing invention is liberating. #1106. Formula 1: Rwanda to bring sport back to Africa

The last time Formula 1 hosted a race in Africa was way back in 1993. But a new track in Rwanda is set to host a Grand Prix in "the early 2030s," continuing the country’s investment in international sport.

After nearly 40 years of false starts, motor racing's premier sport is returning to Africa, after Formula 1 announced on Tuesday that Rwanda would soon host a Grand Prix.

The race will be know as the African Grand Prix after a 10-year contract was signed between the parties. With no suitable track ready, Rwanda will build one in Bugesera, southeast of the capital Kigali. F1 said it will be ready "early in the next decade."

The last time F1 raced in Africa was the South African Grand Prix in 1993. While there has since been plenty of talk of the sport returning to the continent, most often mentioning South Africa itself, nothing concrete had happened, until now.

"Today is a landmark moment for Formula 1," F1 President and chief executive Stefano Domenicali said. "With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the world championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.

"Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."

One of the most vocal proponents of a race in Africa has been seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton. The 41-year-old Black British driver, currently with Ferrari, has said he has been "fighting in the background" for years to have a race in Africa. With the date not yet set in stone for the African Grand Prix, it remains to be seen whether he can prolong his career enough to be on the grid when the lights go out in Rwanda.

For Rwandan President Paul Kagame, the event is "a success and a milestone for the entire continent, especially for the African fans." He added that he hoped it could lead to more F1 events in Africa.

Kagame has been president of Rwanda for 25 years, and essentially ran the country for the six years before that, following the genocide in 1994. He routinely wins over 99% of the vote in elections, and the country is often criticized for its human rights record.

The 68-year-old has bet big on sports. Rwanda has had sponsorship deals with a number of top European football clubs, including Arsenal, Atletico Madrid, Paris Saint-Germain and Bayern Munich. However, fan and media backlash over the deal caused Bayern to drop the commercial element with the country's tourist arm, Visit Rwanda, last year. Arsenal did not renew its deal. Many critics have labeled the policy as sportswashing.

The country also has deals with top US basketball and American football teams, and hosted cycling's Road World Championships last year.

But Formula 1, one of the world's richest sports, will likely be seen as Kagame and Rwanda's biggest sporting coup to date.

#1101. Meet Neuropixels: how probes that track hundreds of brain cells at once are revolutionizing neuroscience

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Diana Kwon is a science writer in Berlin.

Neuropixels probes are designed to record the electrical activity of hundreds of neurons at once. Credit: Allen Institute

In a bright surgical theatre in central London, neurosurgeon Ahmed Toma makes an incision on the side of a woman’s head. Then, he bores a small hole into her skull, revealing a glimpse of the pink, pulsating brain beneath.

Even the unconscious brain can learn — and predict what you’ll say next

Even the unconscious brain can learn — and predict what you’ll say next

Toma is preparing to implant a shunt to drain excess cerebrospinal fluid — a routine treatment for a condition called normal pressure hydrocephalus, in which fluid builds up inside the skull. His patient at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery (NHNN) has also agreed to take part in an experiment: one that involves briefly placing a centimetre-long probe, thinner than a human hair, into her brain. Called Neuropixels, this probe is designed to record the electrical activity of hundreds of neurons at once.

As Toma and a team of researchers carefully insert the probe into the patient’s brain, Mihaly Kollo, a research scientist at the Francis Crick Institute in London, stands nearby, monitoring a multicoloured array of outputs from the probe’s recording sites in real time. After controlling for electrical noise from the operating table and other surgical equipment, Kollo plays an audio sequence of repeating terms — ‘blind spot’, ‘parking spot, ‘piggy bank’ and so on — to examine how the brain represents the transitions between stimuli, and how they are influenced by frequency and familiarity. As the words ring through the theatre, some trigger brain perturbations that sweep across the waveforms representing the probe’s output — a clear sign that it is picking up activity.

Scientists have long conducted experiments during neurosurgery, which offers a rare opportunity to access a living (and often awake) human brain. But Neuropixels probes might provide researchers with the sharpest view of the organ yet.

Since their debut in 2017, Neuropixels have transformed how neuroscientists do electrophysiology experiments in animals, allowing them to record electrical activity from hundreds, sometimes even tens of thousands, of neurons at once. Over the past year, at the NHNN, which is part of the University College London Hospitals, Kollo and his colleagues have been collaborating with neurosurgeons such as Toma to take Neuropixels recordings in people.

Medicine Nobel awarded for brain ‘switch’ that controls neurons with light

Medicine Nobel awarded for brain ‘switch’ that controls neurons with light

There are other ways of surveying single-cell activity in large populations of neurons, such as calcium imaging, which tracks the movement of calcium ions that occurs each time a neuron fires. But these techniques can be too slow to capture the action potentials in certain neurons, or require genetically encoded sensors, limiting their use in some organisms and precluding it in humans.

For people, researchers have relied mostly on devices that sit on the surface of the brain and measure population-level activity, such as high-density electrocorticography. There have also long been tools that can make a relatively small number of recordings at the single-cell level, such as the Utah array — a tiny device studded with miniature needles that penetrate about a millimetre into the brain and that has 96 recording channels.

Pierre Bourdillon, a neurosurgeon at the Adolphe de Rothschild Foundation Hospital in Paris, likens the technological leap for human neuroscience enabled by Neuropixels to the difference between trying to decipher conversations from a single microphone at a busy intersection and listening in on those same discussions using individual microphones attached to the speakers’ collars.

“We’re just starting to get to the level of microphones on individual people,” he says. “For non-human animals, this revolution began about 10–15 years ago. Now we’re just starting to see the first teams using this kind of technology in humans.”

A short walk from the NHNN, at the hospital-turned-research institute known as the Cruciform Building at University College London, neuroscientist Matteo Carandini is applying the most cutting-edge version of Neuropixels technology in organisms with much smaller brains.

His team has been using Neuropixels to record tens of thousands of neurons in mouse brains, sometimes for months at a time. On a sunny Monday afternoon in September, he shows me the set-up for Neuropixels Opto1. This version of the technology, which he has helped to develop, combines electrical recording with optogenetics, a method that allows researchers to switch neurons on and off with light.

Neuroscientists Hayley Bounds (left) and Matteo Carandini examine Neuropixels data.Credit: Matteo Carandini and Hayley Bounds

Carandini was one of the first neuroscientists to use Neuropixels, a device that was designed for research in rodents. The idea began with Tim Harris, a biomedical engineer who arrived at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute’s Janelia Research Campus in Ashburn, Virginia, in 2008 with the task of identifying and developing tools that researchers needed. When he asked his colleagues: ‘What do you want to measure that you can’t?’, he discovered that they were missing probes for conducting long-term, large-scale electrophysiology experiments. In living animals, these involve directly measuring the electrical properties of neurons.

At the time, researchers mostly probed the brain with arrays of twisted four-wire electrodes, which could be combined to record from a few dozen channels at once, or silicon probes, which typically had around 32 recording sites. But they wanted a more comprehensive view of how the cells in the brain work together to perform the organ’s crucial functions — and for that, they would need to collect recordings from many more neurons.

After attempting a few designs on his own, Harris contacted the Interuniversity Microelectronics Centre (Imec), a research institute in Leuven, Belgium, that helped to pioneer some of the world’s most advanced microchips. To Harris’s surprise, Barun Dutta, chief scientist of Imec’s semiconductor technology and systems centre, agreed to take on the task.

How our brains decode speech: special neurons process certain sounds

How our brains decode speech: special neurons process certain sounds

Together, they developed Neuropixels 1.0. The silicon probe comprises 960 recording sites along the hair-thin shank. Each of the recording channels was small enough to capture the action potentials of individual neurons — and 384 of those could be read out in parallel. The shank was attached to a chip the size of a nano SIM card, which holds the electronics required to read, amplify and digitize signals. The outputs could be read with just two wires; this was a major advance at a time when most other devices required each recording channel to have its own wire.

The team reported2 its design in 2017. In that article, Carandini and around three dozen neuroscientists across several laboratories who had tested the device showed that it was possible to insert two of these probes — each weighing about 250 milligrams — into a mouse, allowing them to record around 700 neurons across 5 brain regions at the same time.

Neuropixels 2.0, a smaller, lighter-weight, four-shank probe with 5,120 recording sites (1,536 of which could read out at once), arrived four years later3. (The 1.0 and 2.0 probes are available from Imec for about US$1,700 and $1,800 each, respectively.)

Neuropixels probes have transformed the way neuroscience can be done, says Carandini, who is using the probes to study how the brain processes and uses sensory signals. They enabled the tracking of individual action potentials from thousands of neurons at once and made it possible to record across multiple brain regions in the mouse brain, which is only about one centimetre long.

Using Neuropixels, researchers have found that signals associated with certain sensory, cognitive and motor functions are more widely distributed in the brain than previously thought4. These probes have also enabled scientists to study neural manifolds, the unique patterns of activity that form in populations of brain cells.

Several collaborative efforts known as brain observatories, in which multiple independent teams carry out the same experiments in a standardized manner, have collected vast amounts of Neuropixels data. In one 2025 study5, for example, a dozen labs in the United States and Europe, known as the International Brain Laboratory, came together to collect recordings from more than 620,000 neurons across 279 regions from 139 mice. The result was a brain-wide map of neural activity for both cognitive and motor functions, such as vision, movement and decision-making.

Around 1,700 labs around the world have used Neuropixels in more than two dozen species, including zebra finches, bearded dragons and octopuses. “I was completely taken aback at the variety of species that researchers used these for,” Harris says.

Scientists studying non-human primates were particularly keen: their existing tools either had too few recording channels or could access only the superficial layers of the brain. Harris, Dutta and their colleagues worked with the research community to create Neuropixels 1.0 NHP6, which featured a thicker shank to penetrate the tough membrane around the brain of non-human primates and, at 4 cm in length, could record from deeper structures. (These cost about $4,200 each, according to Dutta.)

Tirin Moore, a neuroscientist at Stanford University in California, who was involved in that effort, says that before Neuropixels, researchers would collect recordings from around two dozen neurons of non-human primates on a good day; now, they routinely record from at least 100. Without these tools, primate neuroscience “would still be in the dark ages”, he says. Moore and his colleagues plan to use the NHP probes to create a high-resolution neural activity map of the visual system of macaque monkeys as part of the Enigma Project, an initiative based at Stanford to record and decode the brain.

A Neuropixels probe records brain activity during surgery to remove part of a person’s brain.Credit: Mihaly Kollo/UCLH

#1099. The hidden treasure in discarded wearable and fast tech

Sales of fast tech like mini fans and disposable e-vapes, as well as wearable health tech such as heart monitors and smartwatches are soaring. They're creating a new e-waste problem but are full of hidden treasure.

From mini fans and the cheap chargers to smartwatches bought as part of a New Year's health kick, some 44% of Europeans own at least six "fast-tech" gadgets. And more than half say they keep unused and broken e-waste items languishing at home or throw them in the regular trash instead of recycling.

That's according to a new report by Brussels-based e-waste association WEEE Forum. It describes fast tech, which is booming, as charging and lighting devices under €10 (circa $11), high-tech items like power banks and fitness trackers, and gadgets and lifestyle appliances like cheap mini blenders and fans, as well as single-use electronic vapes.

"So, these electronics are a bit like fast fashion," Magdalena Charytanowicz, WEEE Forum's Communication Manager, told DW.

Nearly 40% of buyers recalled discarding a fast-tech item without using it at all or within a month of buying it, and nearly 60% said they had used a product for no longer than six months. Yet the vast majority of respondents were generally satisfied with their gadgets despite short-lived functionality.

This suggests consumers accept the "fast-tech bargain" of poor quality that "does the job for a while" and is easily replaced — similar to fast fashion — according to the report.

About 62 million tons of electronics are discarded worldwide annually. "That's the Great Wall of China of e-waste that is produced every year," noted Charytanowicz, adding that the figure is set to grow to 82 million by 2030.

In Europe, roughly 40% of electronic waste is recycled, yet the rate worldwide is just 17%. This means valuable materials are lost, while electronic waste ends up polluting the environment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2022, a million tons of critical raw materials were embedded in the 10.7 million tons of e-waste generated across Europe, including manganese, gold, copper and aluminum.

These materials are at "the center of geopolitical tensions," Charytanowicz said, referring to escalating global tensions over access to rare earths and other critical minerals.

"Even the smallest" devices are worth recycling if they contain a circuit board or battery, she said.

Groups like WEEE Forum say more awareness raising is needed on how to dispose of cheap electronic devices, and that recycling should be made as easy as possible.

But the best way to reduce a product's environmental impact is to extend its lifespan through better design and repair, as recycling raw materials is energy intensive.

Charytonawicz said clearer, harmonized EU rules now under consideration could help improve e-waste collection. The bloc's 20-year-old directive is "not really adapted to the changing reality," she said.

Another growing area of e-waste is digital healthcare. While devices such as diabetes sensors and blood pressure monitors are "transforming healthcare," many are designed to be disposable.

A study published in Nature in December 2025 found sales of wearable healthcare electronics, for example, could reach 2 billion devices annually by 2050, and generate a million tons of e-waste.

Jeremy Faludi, associate professor of sustainable design engineering at TU Delft in the Netherlands, says making health tech — particularly digital devices used in, or issued by hospitals — recyclable or reusable comes with some "much bigger challenges" than normal electronics.

That's in part due to the potential for patient contamination, particularly with digital surgical devices that come into contact with blood or other bodily fluids.

"The way that a lot of things are designed now, you can't recover the stuff because it can't be easily sterilized without the electronics," said Faludi.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He worked on the Digital Health in Circular Economy (DiCE) project, an EU-funded initiative, to help redesign digital healthcare devices to "recover critical materials and reduce environmental impacts without compromising patient safety."

A modular design, for example, allows electronic components to be separated from the parts that need to be replaced between patients, making devices easier to reuse.

The four-year DiCE project, which included citizens, hospitals and manufacturers across nine EU countries, found reusable ECG cables — which connect patients to heart-monitoring equipment — cut environmental impacts by up to 81-94%, for example. The sets are usually designed for single use.

Rules around medical waste can also make reuse and recycling more difficult, particularly when requirements differ between countries and often come down to perceived rather than actual risk, Faludi added. He says some 85% of hospital trash is not infectious but everything ends up in the same bins. Better sorting as well as EU-wide regulations around treating non-infectious hospital waste would help here.

Like with other tech, consumer health devices such as blood pressure and glucose monitors often risk being forgotten in drawers or ending up in the wrong waste, simply because people do not know how to dispose of them, said Charytanowicz of WEEE Forum, which is also involved in DiCE.

Pilot schemes in Belgium, Spain and Slovenia that offered free postal returns and collection machines in public places found that more than 60% of people were willing to return unwanted devices if it was a straightforward process.

"What's really important is the convenience so that it can be integrated in your daily routines," said Charytanowicz, adding that "nudges" such as messages that recycling a device could help the health of another person motivate people to "do the right thing."

#1098. Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

The lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the issues Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N

The last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major issue for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a big day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

“We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

It might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

What they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

James Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU

The roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI

It must be said the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

The whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

#1094. New footage shows how goalkeeper in Spanish footballer's killer collision was fired-up in moments before 'reckless' tackle - as police probe medical team after opening homicide investigation

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER and NATALIA PENZA

Published: 05:13 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 08:28 EDT, 4 November 2026

New footage has revealed the tense moments before goalkeeper Jesus Owono launched a 'reckless' tackle that led to the death of Tenerife footballer Jesus de Miguel.

FC Andorra goalkeeper Owono collided with opposing striker De Miguel in the latter stages of a hotly contested 2-2 draw in Spain's second division on Monday.

De Miguel immediately collapsed following the devastating blow in which Owono's knee appeared to strike the forward in the chest. He passed away in the early hours of Tuesday morning.

A homicide squad has launched an investigation as court officials explained any death 'not resulting from natural causes' automatically triggers a judicial investigation, with police now also probing the medical response to the incident.

Now, new footage taken from the stands has revealed how a fired-up Owono behaved in the moments leading up to the devastating collision.

The video shows how Owono had made his way to the other end of the pitch to get involved in a confrontation following a red card for opposing goalkeeper Dani Martin, before appearing to motion for him to make his way off the field of play.

Footage has revealed the heated build-up to the tackle that led to the death of Jesus de Miguel, which showed goalkeeper Jesus Owono arguing with his rival goalkeeper. (Source: X/Eldense_)

Fans have commented in Owono's involvement in an argument with opposing goalkeeper Dani Martin, who was sent off in the closing stages of the match (Source: X/Eldense_)

Martin and Owono appeared to continue their argument as they exchanged gestures as the Tenerife shot-stopper departed the scene.

The footage then captured Owono's wild celebrations - in which he leapt into the air and punched his fist - as Andorra FC scored an 88th minute equaliser.

'Here you have the images prior to the action by goalkeeper Owono, in the parts where he's not in focus — in one of them, he's confronting and saying things to the rival goalkeeper, and in the other, celebrating the goal right in the face of the Tenerife stands,' one fan wrote.

'He's a repeat offender when it comes to this kind of behavior.'

Another said: 'There isn't anyone from those of us who were in the stadium who didn't agree with the opinion that the entry was reckless. That it was an assault. It's clear that he didn't want the final outcome, but it's also clear that it wasn't an isolated incident.'

'I'm right behind that goal! Owono was completely unhinged! He came all the way to the rival goal to confront Dani, the Tenerife goalkeeper, over Lautaro's red card, and started gesticulating wildly at Dani to get him off the field after being sent off! This guy was totally out of his mind,' a third posted.

Former Real Madrid and Spain international goalkeeper Santiago Canizares, speaking on El Partidazo de COPE, conceded he believed Owono used ‘excessive force’ when going for the challenge.

Canizares, however, offered a defence of Owono by explaining the goalkeeper’s likely thought process and explained that they typically use their knees as protection and to help avoid collisions.

‘It's a goal-scoring opportunity, and what Owono has in his head is “I have to contest that ball,” ball or player,' Canizares said.

De Miguel died on Tuesday morning following a horrifying clash with Andorra FC goalkeeper Jesus Owono

The striker was struck in the chest by Owono's flying knee as he attempted to clear the ball near the halfway line

‘For me, the problem is that Owono uses excessive force, and he lacks the physical dexterity to pull himself back when he sees he's won the duel.

‘He goes all out and goes all out until the end. That physical dexterity is key when only one of the two is contesting.

‘What happens in this case is that I think the momentum causes the knee to rise due to the force and excessive speed it brings.’

Andorra FC defender Lautaro Spatz has also defended his team-mate, writing that the goalkeeper has been 'deeply affected’ by the tragedy.

‘There are moments when football loses its meaning. Moments that mark you forever and make you realise how fragile life can be,’ Spatz wrote in a statement shared on social media.

‘What we went through is something none of us will ever forget. A tragedy that has left us completely broken, speechless, and with a sadness that is difficult to explain.

‘First and foremost, I want to express my deepest condolences and all my love to Jesús’s family, friends, and loved ones, as well as to the entire Tenerife community and the entire football family. Since yesterday, the entire FC Andorra squad has been shocked, devastated, and deeply affected by what has happened. It is a tragedy we never imagined we would experience on a football pitch,' he said.

‘I also want to say a few words to my teammate, goalkeeper, and friend, who is deeply affected by what happened. Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is. We know how much he is suffering right now and that he would never intend to hurt anyone.

‘In football, unforeseen events occur, but no one can imagine that one of them could end with such tragic consequences. Today, football doesn't matter. All that remains is to offer our condolences, show the utmost respect, and send all our strength to the family and to all those suffering this terrible loss. Rest in peace, Demi.'

Police investigating De Miguel's death are now probing the emergency medical response as well as the possibility rival goalie Jesus Owono's horror tackle could be involuntary manslaughter.

It emerged yesterday homicide squad officers based in the Tenerife capital Santa Cruz had launched a probe as court officials explained any death 'not resulting from natural causes' automatically triggers a judicial investigation.

Legal experts have said they don't expect the ongoing investigation to lead to criminal charges against Andorra FC goalkeeper Owono because the clash occurred during open play, although he is expected to be hit with a lengthy ban.

But overnight it emerged the police probe will also review the medical response to Monday's emergency and seek to address questions about whether Jesus de Miguel was given oxygen on the pitch and whether a defibrillator was used from the outset as well as issues around the assistance he received during his ambulance transfer.

The 30-year-old father-of-one died yesterday morning at Nuestra Senora Candelaria University Hospital after his second-division club revealed his neurological condition had worsened.

Medical personnel involved in the footballer's care are expected to be questioned and detectives will sift through medical reports as part of the probe.

Police investigating the death of CD Tenerife footballer Jesus de Miguel are probing the emergency medical response

Legal experts have said they don't expect the ongoing investigation to lead to criminal charges against Andorra FC goalkeeper Owono

Well-placed sources told local press overnight there were 'certain discrepancies within the reports, or potential inaccuracies when compared to other evidence in the case' such as video footage recorded and posted on social media.

Respected island newspaper El Dia said: 'Among the issues currently under investigation, which according to sources remained unresolved as of yesterday, is whether the medical team who rushed from the sidelines to the centre of the pitch carrying a stretcher, a spinal board, and an Automated External Defibrillator to attend to the player, acted with due diligence during the more than six minutes they spent on the pitch before placing him on the spinal board for transport to an ambulance, which was stationed at one of the stadium access gates on La Mutine Street.'

It added: 'Investigators are also looking into an even more striking question.

'After a Guedel airway, a curved, semi-rigid oropharyngeal tube, was inserted into the player's mouth following his loss of consciousness, to prevent his tongue from obstructing his airway, was he also provided with oxygen during the resuscitation efforts on the pitch, as is required by protocol?

'According to sources, efforts are still underway to gather all available evidence to determine whether De Miguel was administered oxygen, either via a bag-valve mask (Ambu bag) or a face mask connected to one of the oxygen cylinders kept pitchside at the stadium.

'Sources indicate that this remains unresolved, at least regarding the medical care provided on the field of play.

'Furthermore, footage of the player being transported on a spinal board suggests that oxygen was not being administered during that process.

'Additionally, during the evacuation from the centre of the pitch to the ambulance, the player was carried on a spinal board by individuals who were moving at a jog.

Tributes have been paid to De Miguel outside the entrance to Tenerife's stadium

'The manner in which the patient was transported, which should never have been carried out in such a way, was highly dangerous to their physical well-being.'

Equatorial Guinea international Owono, who has lived in Spain since he was eight, was red-carded for kneeing Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel in the chest near the halfway line late into stoppage time. The match was suspended when the two sides were drawing 2-2.

Tragic Jesus, whose partner Maria and one-year-old daughter Carla were watching from the stands, was reportedly revived by paramedics on the pitch after going into cardiac arrest before being rushed to hospital.

His club confirmed around 9.30am local time yesterday morning he had died at a hospital in the Tenerife capital Santa Cruz about 8am, saying they were 'heartbroken' and had a 'lump in their throats'.

It said in a statement, after revealing earlier the footballer's neurological condition had worsened: 'Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats, and unable to believe this is true, CD Tenerife announces the tragic passing of Jesus de Miguel Alameda, which occurred this Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 8am.

'There are no words of comfort, there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow.

'We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire 'tinerfeñismo' community, who today mourn this cruel outcome.

Owono is reportedly intending to apologise directly to de Miguel's family for his challenge and has made his social media private following abusive chants and messages he received (Source: Instagram/Jesus Owono)

Owono is reportedly seeking to apologise to Jesus de Miguel's family before making any kind of public statement.

FC Andorra, reacting to news of the Tenerife striker's death in hospital, said yesterday morning: 'Heartbroken and devastated, we wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife.

Later today Jesus de Miguel's body is expected to be flown to the Spanish mainland so his funeral can take place in the town where his parents hail from.

The 30-year-old footballer's mum and dad travelled to Tenerife after being told about the severity of his injuries before confirmation this morning he had died in an island hospital.

They will now make the reverse trip to Madrid before travelling to Navahermosa in the province of Toledo 80 miles south-west of the Spanish capital which they have chosen as the place for the player's funeral.

Jesus's club revealed the location yesterday afternoon but said it was unable to say at this stage when exactly it would be.

Town hall officials in Navahermosa, which has a population of just over 3,500 inhabitants, said immediately after learning of the footballer's death: 'Since yesterday, we had held onto the hope that Jesus might overcome the toughest match of his life. However, we woke up today to the worst possible news.

'On behalf of the town hall, we wish to express our deepest sorrow at this tragic outcome. We want to extend all our love, support, and affection to his family, friends, and everyone who is feeling this loss today.

'There are no words that can ease such profound pain, but please know that we are by your side and that we share in your sadness.

'Jesus, you have always been, and will always remain, a source of pride for us.

'Today, with broken hearts, we must say goodbye, but we will hold onto your memory. Rest in peace.'

Emiliano Garcia-Page, president of Spain's Castilla-La Mancha region which includes Navahermosa and the province of Toledo where a train crash last Wednesday claimed the lives of 69 people, added in his own statement: 'I am at a loss for words; the passing of footballer Jesus de Miguel, while doing what he loved most and what he had fought so hard for, playing football, is heartbreaking news.

'My thoughts are with his family, who hail from the municipality of Navahermosa in the province of Toledo. My deepest condolences.'

The entire CD Tenerife squad will travel to Navahermosa to pay their last respects to their teammate.

Flags outside the town hall flew at half mast today.

The National Police in the island capital Santa Cruz has yet to release an official statement about its ongoing probe.

A minute's silence was held before Champions League matches in memory of De Miguel on Tuesday

But a force spokesman said yesterday evening: 'An investigation is underway into the circumstances surrounding the incident which led to Jesus de Miguel's death which is being conducted by the homicide unit.

'It has been opened because the death was not the result of natural causes and it will seek to determine whether in terms of the law, an involuntary manslaughter could have been committed.'

The report police draft as a result of their probe will be submitted to a local judge whose job it will be to decide whether to take the matter further.

A Canary Islands court source described the collision between the two footballers as 'an accidental collision on the playing field.'

But he added: 'Any death not resulting from natural causes, referred to as a 'forensic death,' whether due to an accident or other factors, automatically triggers a judicial investigation, which is the case here.'

Court officials said this morning they weren't able to comment on when they expected to receive the police report into the drama.

One said: 'At the moment the investigation is still in the hands of police who will submit their report to a court in Santa Cruz once officers have completed their work.'

#1091. Man Utd the masters of self-destruction as pressure piles on Carrick

So where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, said he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

Chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

The problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

Take nothing away from Morgan Rogers – his 40yd dash from the edge of the centre circle in United’s half to the six-yard box and the finish that followed were top notch. But where was the challenge? How could not a single player in red have stood in his path? “Come on Morgan, run through us buddy” seemed to be the message.

By the end, with Estevao – making the most of a first league start of the season – running riot and Chelsea smelling blood, Carrick would have been relieved the scoreline was not worse. Michael Carrick said he expects to be in charge of Manchester United next week despite Lisandro Martinez’s moment of madness leaving the club mired in a relegation battle and on their worst run for 38 years.

United were urged to sell Martinez after the controversial Argentina defender was sent off for elbowing Wesley Fofana as Carrick accused his side of “unravelling” as they slumped to a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea.

It left United without a win in nine matches, their worst run since 1988, and at risk of being sucked into the relegation zone. They have won just two of 13 games this season.

The Old Trafford hierarchy gave Carrick a stay of execution in midweek and, when asked if he expected to still to be at the helm when United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, the head coach replied: “Yes. I’m just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now.”

Having been booked moments earlier for a foul on Morgan Rogers, Martinez was sent off for a second yellow. The incident came less than three weeks after the Argentinian was fined and publicly apologised for attacking United director of football Jason Wilcox and the board over transfer policy and was the latest in a series of mistakes from him on the pitch this season.

Joe Cole, the former Chelsea and England forward, believes United must get rid of Martinez.

“Whatever the next Manchester United looks like, Lisandro Martinez has run his course,’ Cole said on TNT Sports. “He’s at the scene of the crime too often for Manchester United and is at fault for moments and goals like that. So that’s probably his time done.”

Carrick refused to publicly criticise Martinez but admitted his dismissal was a “huge moment” and felt his team “unravelled” in the second period.

“Things have gone against us in a big way,” the United manager said. “It’s unravelled quickly. There’s a lot of emotion right now. It’s a huge moment in the game. Sometimes you get setbacks in games and you’ve got to deal with that better. I’ve not seen it [the Martinez incident] back so I don’t know if it was [a red card] or not. He’s gone to it and the referee gave that decision, but it’s a big moment.”

Asked if there would be a stigma attached to United potentially dropping into the relegation zone, Carrick added: “Not for me, no.”

And when asked how his players would deal with a relegation battle, Carrick added: “We’ve got to keep moving forward and winning games. There’s no words I’m going to explain to you now that makes any difference, it’s not going to change it. We’ve got to move forward and win matches.”

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Chelsea, who start the day in fifth, and 16th-placed Manchester United at Stamford Bridge. On Sunday and Monday it seemed certain that Michael Carrick would be relieved of his duties before today’s game but has survived for now, hoping to turn things around in the no man’s land that sometimes resembles a vote of confidence and at others a stay of execution.

Thirty years ago when Newcastle United were coming off the bridle in the title race with Manchester United, Alex Ferguson, as he then was, accused a Leeds team, who had been in freefall since the new year, of professional malpractice when they put in a rare display of passionate commitment and tenacity at Old Trafford in a 1-0 defeat.

“Why are they not in the top six?” asked Ferguson. “To me they’re cheating their manager. You wait and see the difference when they play Newcastle.” The hate between the Leeds and Manchester united fanbases was such, he implied, that they had decided to put a shift in because, for once, they feared the consequences if they had not. It seems to this observer that the boot is now on the other foot. These Manchester United players roused themselves to fight at Elland Road then chucked it in against Como and Bournemouth. If that’s not “cheating their manager”, what is?

Carrick will have to hope that some of the old hostility between Chelsea and Manchester United might encourage the players to run about a bit this afternoon and, at the very least, get stuck in rather than crumple spinelessly as they did last week. I doubt it would be enough to save Carrick’s job in the medium term but at least it would address whether they could stake a claim to be part of the rebuilding process.

As for Chelsea, who were awful in defeat by Brentford and Spurs either side of impressive victories over Bournemouth and at Everton, they need to find some defensive solidity, discipline and a way of terrorising defences in the absence of Joao Pedro. They are a work in progress still, in the fifth year of the hedge fund hegemony. For all that attacking talent and Moises Caicedo’s ability to steamroll midfielders, their defence does not inspire confidence and last year’s petulance continues to simmer.

#1089. Five overlooked steps to identify new epidemics, fast

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Serge Tonen-Wolyec is a coordinator at the Interdisciplinary Center for Translational Research in Medicine and Health Sciences, Bunia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and professor of infectious diseases in the Faculty of Medicine, University of Bunia.

Laurent Belec is a virologist in the Faculty of Medicine, Paris Cité University, Paris, France, and in the Department of Microbiology, Assistance Publique-Hôpitaux de Paris, Paris.

Identifying people who have an infection and keeping them isolated can be key to managing emerging diseases. Credit: Lisa Maree Williams/Getty

The current deadly outbreak of Ebola in Africa is the latest in a string of diseases to grab headlines in recent years — from COVID-19 to mpox and hantavirus. Outbreaks are easier to control if they can be detected early and contained. But many emerging, evolving or unfamiliar diseases fall through the cracks of current surveillance systems.

Better diagnostics could have limited this Ebola outbreak

Better diagnostics could have limited this Ebola outbreak

Epidemics are tracked using three approaches. First, event-based tracking monitors local information sources — media reports, social-media posts, community alerts and health-worker reports — to detect early signals of an outbreak. Second, genomic sequencing is used to confirm a pathogen’s identity1,2. And third, syndromic surveillance looks for people at risk of being infected, by identifying and monitoring individuals who present with characteristic symptoms.

But these strategies don’t account for the fact that an emerging pathogen might present with unusual or atypical symptoms. The presentation of symptoms can change over time, as a pathogen evolves3, and they can also vary between people, who might have different levels of immunity. And co-infections that present with similar symptoms to those caused by a pathogen can obscure diagnoses4.

This gap in surveillance has caused problems time and again.

For example, during the early 2020 wave of SARS-CoV-2, initial diagnoses relied on the presence of fever and respiratory distress5,6. In many countries, it took months for another common symptom, loss of smell, to be accepted as an indicator of COVID-19, allowing individuals to bypass isolation protocols. New variants of the virus brought with them different symptoms: Omicron was associated with cold- and influenza-like symptoms more often than it was with the loss of smell or taste7.

COVID’s origins: what we do and don’t know

COVID’s origins: what we do and don’t know

In the 2022 mpox outbreak, which affected mainly Europe and North America, some individuals with the infection presented with genital and anal sores, rather than the widespread rash associated with classic mpox. These people were initially misdiagnosed with other conditions, including sexually transmitted infections, potentially delaying recognition and public-health action8.

Similarly, Nipah virus is proving hard to diagnose in clinics in Bangladesh and India because its symptoms can shift between brain-tissue inflammation (causing confusion and seizures) and breathing difficulties9.

Unless clinicians recognize that unusual symptoms warrant investigation, even the most advanced tracking systems cannot keep up. Here we set out five steps to improve health systems’ abilities to recognize emerging pathogens. Together, these steps form a loop in which clinical signals are detected, validated, translated into surveillance and diagnostic guidance, then rapidly fed back to front-line clinicians. We call this approach ‘symptom preparedness’.

Formal mechanisms are needed for clinicians to act on the intuition that they are dealing with something unusual, such as several people presenting with the same unrecognized set of symptoms. National public-health agencies and health ministries should provide reporting procedures for documenting such ‘clinical drift’ through existing digital surveillance tools, such as the online platform District Health Information Software 2 (DHIS2).

To prevent false-positive alerts, a second senior clinician or hospital epidemiologist would need to verify that the cluster is atypical. Clinicians could then run an algorithm on DHIS2, or an equivalent tool, that uses statistical checks to confirm that these symptoms are unlikely to be caused by routine seasonal illnesses. Once verified, these reports would automatically trigger localized digital alerts to national public-health intelligence centres, where epidemiologists would cross-reference regional data before formal surveillance measures are activated10.

Machine-learning models that are trained on temporally and geographically labelled clinical data might help physicians to detect atypical cases in the future, by identifying people whose symptoms differ from patterns normally observed in the same population. The models should not provide a diagnosis, but could flag cases that warrant further examination. In this way, artificial-intelligence tools would augment rather than replace clinical judgement11,12.

Low-resource settings might lack the facilities needed to run an AI model. But health workers could submit anonymized clinical information to a country-wide centralized AI system through a phone app, SMS-based reporting system or existing electronic registries. The AI system would return an alert when needed.

Public-health authorities should transition away from using only standardized clinical criteria provided by agencies such as the World Health Organization to classify disease cases. Instead, they should adopt dynamic, tiered case definitions that distinguish suspected, probable and confirmed cases.

AI biohazard hype must not divert attention from the real risks we face now

AI biohazard hype must not divert attention from the real risks we face now

Committees of epidemiological specialists would stratify diagnostic criteria into tiers and update them dynamically — on a weekly or rolling basis — as real-time clinical data emerge10. For example, the standard symptoms of mpox conventionally included a generalized rash. If a dynamic diagnosis system had been available in 2022, public-health authorities could, within days of recognizing atypical clusters, have expanded the ‘suspected case’ definition to include localized genital sores. This rapid adaptation could have helped to identify misdiagnosed individuals sooner.
